production_notes: Principles only, not legal advice. The voiceover states no legal conclusion as settled and says so twice. Legal review of this script is recommended before release.

[VERIFY] [REGION] Copyright protection and ownership of AI-generated images, the role of human contributions such as selecting, arranging and editing, likeness rights and AI-labelling requirements differ by country and are changing. The voiceover presents each as a question to check, with 'in many places' or 'may'.

[VERIFY] [VERSION] Commercial-use terms for Gemini, Adobe Firefly and Canva, differences between free and paid plans, and any company claims about training data (for example, claims of licensed training images) must be checked against current official terms. The voiceover names no tool's terms and repeats no company claim.

[VERIFY] Content.md mentions SynthID (an invisible watermark Google describes for some of its AI images) and Content Credentials (which Adobe describes, based on the C2PA open standard). These names are left out of the voiceover and slides until confirmed for each tool; the voiceover says only that some tools add signals. Add them to scene 9's slide after verification if wanted.

The worked example is hypothetical and uses no named legal disputes, as agreed in the curriculum. Tomasz, his Warsaw studio and the organic juice client are fictional. The famous athlete in the example is never named or shown.
No real people, logos, brand names or copyrighted characters in any slide image. The bias slide uses generated, fictional families.
No hero B-roll: slides and one stock scene carry the visuals.

Hook.voiceover: Your image looks great, and the client loves it. But can they put it on a billboard? Can they stop a competitor from copying it? Does anyone need to know it was made with AI? Before you publish, ask the right questions.

Explain.voiceover: First, an important point. This lesson teaches principles, not legal advice. The rules are different in different countries, and they are still changing. For a real client campaign, ask a qualified legal adviser in your country.

slide.title: Copyright, Licences and Ethics
slide.body: AI Image Generation and Visual Design · Lesson 10 of 12. Banner: Principles, not legal advice. Rules differ by country and are changing.

Explain.voiceover: One, ownership and copyright. In many places, copyright protects work created by people. Whether a mostly AI-made image can be protected, and who may own it, differs by country. Your own contributions, like selecting and editing, may matter. So keep records of your prompts and edits. They show your creative work.

slide.title: 1 Ownership and copyright
slide.body: Copyright often protects work made by people · Protection and ownership of AI images: differs by country, under discussion · Selecting, arranging and editing may matter · Keep records of prompts and edits

Explain.voiceover: Two, tool licence terms. Each tool has its own terms of use. They say whether you may use images commercially, what rights you give the tool company, and whether free and paid plans differ. Terms change, so read them before each client project. And treat any company claims about training as statements to check yourself.

slide.title: 2 Tool licence terms
slide.body: Commercial use allowed? · What rights do you give the tool company? · Free and paid plans may differ · Terms change: read them before each project · Company claims about training: check the official terms

Explain.voiceover: Three, people's likeness. Do not create images that look like real, identifiable people without their consent, and never make images that could mislead viewers about a real person. Four, trademarks and characters. Keep other companies' logos, brand names and copyrighted characters out of your prompts and images.

slide.title: 3 Likeness · 4 Trademarks
slide.body: Left: silhouette of a person with a crossed-out ID card: no real, identifiable people without consent. Right: blank crossed-out logo shape and character outline: no logos, brand names or characters.

Explain.voiceover: Five, bias. Models can repeat stereotypes, like showing only one gender as doctors. Review who appears in your set, and prompt for the variety your audience really has. Six, disclosure. Some tools add visible or invisible signals that show an image was made with AI. Some platforms ask for labels. Do not try to remove these signals.

slide.title: 5 Bias · 6 Disclosure
slide.body: Bias: review who appears; prompt for real variety · Disclosure: some tools add visible or invisible AI signals · Some platforms ask for AI labels · Never remove these signals

Explain.voiceover: Publishing an AI image is like using a rented car for business. You can drive it, but the agreement says where you may go and for what purpose. Before a long trip, you read the agreement, and if something is unclear, you ask.

Demonstrate.voiceover: Here is a hypothetical case. Tomasz is a freelance designer in Warsaw, Poland. A small organic juice company asks him for ten AI images for a national poster campaign. Before he starts, he does five things.

slide.title: A hypothetical case
slide.body: Tomasz · freelance designer · Warsaw, Poland. Client: a small organic juice company (fictional). Brief: 10 AI images for a national poster campaign.

Demonstrate.voiceover: First, he opens the terms of use for his tool, and finds the section about commercial use. He notes whether his free plan allows it, and whether paid plans have different rules. Second, he tells the client the images were made with AI, and asks whether they need exclusive rights. He explains that he cannot promise copyright protection.

slide.title: Tomasz's checks, 1 and 2
slide.body: 1. Read the tool's commercial-use terms: free plan vs paid plans · 2. Tell the client the images are AI-made · Ask about exclusive rights · No promise of copyright protection

Demonstrate.voiceover: Third, he finds a prompt line that describes a famous athlete. He removes it, and writes a runner in her forties instead. Fourth, he reviews the draft set for bias. All four family images show the same type of family, so he adds variety.

slide.title: Tomasz's checks, 3 and 4
slide.body: Left: prompt line crossed out 'a famous athlete' (no name shown) → 'a runner in her forties'. Right: four generated family images, first all similar, then a varied set of fictional families.

Demonstrate.voiceover: Fifth, he writes down the questions he cannot answer, and books a short call with a legal adviser. He does not guess.

slide.title: Tomasz's check 5
slide.body: Write down open questions · Book a short call with a legal adviser · Don't guess

Demonstrate.voiceover: A common mistake is to think, the tool let me make it, so I can use it however I want. The tool's ability says nothing about whether you may publish the image. Another mistake is to trust a summary on a blog or social post. Always read the current official terms yourself.
Demonstrate.on_screen_text: Can make it is not may use it

Recap.voiceover: Let's recap. First, copyright and ownership of AI images differ by country and are changing, so treat them as questions to check, not settled facts. Second, read each tool's current terms before a client project, and keep records of your prompts and edits. Third, avoid real people's likeness, logos and characters, check your set for bias, and do not remove AI labels.

slide.title: Key takeaways
slide.body: 1. Copyright differs by country: questions, not facts. 2. Read current terms; keep records. 3. No likeness, logos or characters; check bias; keep AI labels.

CTA.voiceover: Now it is your turn. In the exercise below, you will read the commercial-use section of one tool's official terms, and write three questions for a legal adviser. It takes about twenty-five minutes. Next comes the capstone. In the next lesson, Capstone: Planning Your Brand Visual Set, you start your own campaign. See you there.
